ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 5 — Annual Wellness Visit, Subsequent — Voltaire — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Subsequent annual wellness visit, a week after the bladder cancer diagnosis. [S]

Voltaire returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit, six days after he learned that the bladder tumor is a muscle-invasive squamous cell carcinoma and chose weekly radiotherapy. The planning scan was done yesterday and the first treatment is tomorrow. His fever settled within two days of starting cefpodoxime, and he finished the seven-day course two days ago; the culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to it. He has voided without a catheter for six days, getting up twice at night. He takes acetaminophen three times a day and has used two half tablets of oxycodone in six days, for bladder spasm in the evening; he keeps them in a locked box. He completed the health risk assessment beforehand. He has had no falls. He has cut his coffee to three cups a day and sleeps about five hours without the sleep aid. He is still at work on his play. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1778-04-28; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Thin (BMI 18.5), alert, and quick; blood pressure 126/70 mmHg seated and 120/68 mmHg standing
Whispered-voice test passed on both sides
Regular rhythm; no murmur; no edema
Soft; mild suprapubic tenderness; bladder not palpable
Timed Up and Go 13 seconds with his stick; rises from a chair using his arms
Oriented; Mini-Cog 4 of 5 (recall 2 of 3, clock normal)
Wry and engaged; mood "steady, mostly"; no hopelessness
Visible blood in the urine for three weeks with clots, and a weak stream, straining, and frequent small voids, in a man of 83; under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem echoing his documented urinary complaints and last illness; superseded by the diagnosis at the third chronic-care visit.
Chronic urinary retention with overflow (post-void residual 460 mL at intake), worsened by a nightly anticholinergic sleep aid; drained by an indwelling catheter
S — Synthetic finding echoing the strangury and catheterization documented in his last weeks.
Acute kidney injury from bladder outlet obstruction (creatinine 1.68 mg/dL, from 1.1 mg/dL a year earlier)
S — Synthetic finding; it echoes, without asserting, the later encyclopedia term uremia.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms: prostate about 78 mL on CT, enlarged, firm, and smooth on examination, PSA 6.4 ng/mL with a PSA density of 0.08; no prostate biopsy, by shared decision
S — Synthetic diagnosis echoing the very large prostate described at the 1778 autopsy; whether that prostate was malignant is unknown (CLM-0012).

Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, keratinizing, posterior wall extending to the dome, muscle-invasive with extravesical extension (clinical stage cT3b N0 M0, stage IIIA), pure squamous histology without a urothelial component; treated with palliative-intent hypofractionated radiotherapy by shared decision

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis confirmed by resection pathology. His bladder disease at autopsy is documented (D); calling it squamous cell carcinoma is a 2025 retrospective interpretation (R, disputed).
Chronic constipation, lifelong by his account, with long use of laxatives and self-given enemas
S — Synthetic modern problem echoing his documented colic, purges, and enemas; no diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease is made.
Febrile catheter-associated urinary tract infection with Escherichia coli, five days after bladder tumor resection; treated with cefpodoxime and a catheter change; resolved
S — Synthetic intercurrent infection; it echoes, without asserting, the infected urine described in his last weeks (CLM-0009).

Health risk assessment reviewed and the personalized prevention plan updated for a frail man of 83 starting cancer treatment: the plan now favors vaccines, falls prevention, nutrition, and planning for future care over cancer screening. text.paragraph: Guideline basis: American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023); Prostate Cancer: Screening (2018); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, urologic cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia monographs (2026); Medicare Preventive Services reference: visit templates, screening cascades, and documentation elements (2026); Adult Immunization Schedule by Age (2026); Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024); Colorectal Cancer: Screening (2021); Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: Screening (2019); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018)

Follow-up: Radiotherapy starts tomorrow. Chronic-care review in eight days as planned, with blood tests and a bladder scan. Home physical therapy this week. Next annual wellness visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 1778-05-06: two-week review during weekly radiotherapy: symptoms, kidney function, voiding, and opioid safety. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 25 minutes, with his consent, prompted by the cancer diagnosis. He names a long-time younger colleague as his health care agent and signed the state directive form today. He wants treatment that keeps him at home and able to write, including radiotherapy and treatment of infections, and a short hospital stay for a reversible problem such as bleeding or blocked urine. He would not want resuscitation, a breathing machine, or major surgery, and he wants comfort-focused care at home if the cancer progresses. A portable medical order for life-sustaining treatment was completed with these choices (do not attempt resuscitation; selective treatment). He wants frank information and asked that his medicines for pain and sleep be kept simple and prescribed by one clinician. [S]
